rows.title: Musk’s fantasy for a future where work is optional just got more real: U.K. minister calls for universal basic income to cushion AI-related job losses
rows.standfirst: This week, Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei warned of “unusually painful” disruptions to the labor market as a result of AI.

rows.title: CEO of $1.25 billion AI company says he hires Gen Z because they’re ‘less biased’ than older generations—too much knowledge is actually bad, he warns
rows.standfirst: The founder and CEO of $1.25 billion AI identity verification platform Incode, Ricardo Amper, says Gen Z’s naivety is actually a powerful resource.

rows.title: Trump’s plan to make housing affordable is faltering
rows.standfirst: “We’re not going to destroy the value of their homes so somebody who didn’t work very hard can buy a home,” Trump said.

rows.title: In 2026, many employers are ditching merit-based pay bumps in favor of ‘peanut butter raises’
rows.standfirst: Bucking the trend of rewarding only top staffers, around 44% of companies are planning fixed pay bumps spread out evenly to all their employees—and it could help low-income workers.

rows.title: $15 billion tech CEO says she doesn’t know what jobs will look like in 2 years—but she’s still pushing her son into computer science
rows.standfirst: HubSpot CEO Yamini Rangan admits tech jobs are changing fast—but says Gen Z shouldn’t ditch higher education: “Depth in an area, combined with learning how to learn, is what really matters.”

rows.title: Meet the Palm Beach billionaire who paid $2 million for a private White House visit with Trump
rows.standfirst: “A presidency that seems up for sale to the highest bidder,” one watchdog warned.

rows.title: Americans are so broke and housing is so expensive that ‘rent now, pay later’ is on the rise
rows.standfirst: Companies such as Flex, Livble and, more recently, Affirm, say breaking rent into multiple payments can help renters manage cash flow. Beware, experts say.

rows.title: Kevin O’Leary blasts attacks on billionaire entrepreneurs as a ‘huge mistake’—He says they don’t get enough credit for the jobs they’ve created
rows.standfirst: ‘Shark Tank’ star Kevin O’Leary says mega-billionaires like Michael Dell and Warren Buffett actually stimulate the labor market and ‘give all their wealth back’ after success.

rows.title: Having a college degree still matters for being one of the wealthier Americans, New York Fed says
rows.standfirst: The spending divide is visible in the past three years of data, the New York Fed says, and college degrees matter a lot.

rows.title: PepsiCo is cutting prices for snacks like Doritos by ‘up to 15%’ to appease customers pinched by the K-shaped economy
rows.standfirst: The average price of PepsiCo products climbed about 4% in the last two years after skyrocketing by double-digit percentages in 2022 and 2023.

rows.title: Scott Bessent’s ‘gotcha’ moment on Trump’s tariffs and inflation: He denies writing ‘tariffs are inflationary’ in letter to hedge fund investors
rows.standfirst: In 2024 Bessent wrote: “Tariffs are inflationary and would strengthen the dollar.” He denied this before the House Financial Services Committee.

rows.title: Forget a degree—$30 billion defense startup Anduril will fast-track your job application if you can win its AI drone-flying contest
rows.standfirst: Anduril founder Palmer Luckey admits he likes to hire people with experience off the beaten path—and he’s now scouting new talent via a drone-flying contest.

rows.title: Metals are the new oil, JD Vance pitches to America: ‘There’s no realer thing than critical minerals’
rows.standfirst: Trump officials are pitching a new framework to think about raw minerals. It’s not actually new.

rows.title: Rocket CEO says U.S. mortgage industry is a ‘tale of two cities.’ His booming business shows a broader reality for American homebuyers
rows.standfirst: “Mortgage rates dropped to the lowest that they’ve been in the past three years,” Varun Krishna said, “and Rocket was right there to capitalize.”

rows.title: Your Super Bowl party can beat inflation, Wells Fargo says. Just double down on wings and guac and skip the beef
rows.standfirst: “If you can’t get excited about a big plate of chicken wings and cheesy nachos with guacamole, I don’t know what’s going to make you happy.”

rows.title: Meet a 27-year-old software engineer who turned a 1.0 GPA in high school into a six-figure career at American Express
rows.standfirst: Per Scholas has been bridging the skills divide for 30 years.

rows.title: Trump may hand out fatter tax refunds this year, but whether a short-staffed IRS can get it to you is a different matter, watchdog warns
rows.standfirst: Delays in processing tax returns can be especially perilous for low-income households.

rows.title: Trump boasts that tariffs are an American economic miracle. The real data tells a different story
rows.standfirst: Here’s a look at the facts around Trump’s assessment of tariffs driving economic growth.

rows.title: The U.S. construction industry’s need for labor is soaring and will need half a million new workers next year while AI giants ramp up spending
rows.standfirst: The Associated Builders and Contractors said the industry will need to bring in 456,000 new workers in 2027, up 30.7% from the 349,000 needed this year.

rows.title: We may be looking at the housing affordability crisis all wrong. Higher earners are driving home prices, not lack of supply, researchers say
rows.standfirst: Rather than a lack of supply, housing affordability “may primarily be about differences in income growth at the top of the distribution relative to the middle.”

rows.title: Bill Gates is shedding houses that are part of his $132 million Xanadu 2.0 compound—a reversal from his feelings about downsizing
rows.standfirst: The latest listing goes to show how much of the exclusive hillside neighborhood Gates has acquired during the past three decades.

rows.title: Grocery prices have surged 25% in Colorado since the pandemic with Kroger and Walmart sharing half the market. Enter Aldi
rows.standfirst: Food prices are a more acute problem in Colorado than in many U.S. states due to a highly concentrated retail and supply chain system.

rows.title: Trump’s plan to send home prices higher will help him with baby boomer voters ahead of midterm elections but could spark a ‘generational war’
rows.standfirst: In the 2024 presidential election, 81% of Trump’s voters were homeowners, according to AP VoteCast data.

rows.title: Super Bowl champion Sam Darnold says his plumber dad played with him every day after work, no matter how tough his day was—and that taught him resilience
rows.standfirst: Seahawks quarterback Sam Darnold’s working-class parents taught him how to be resilient and consistent. It’s led him through career setbacks to his recent Super Bowl win.

rows.title: Which class of mortgage holder are you? Only 20% are in the elite pre-2022 camp
rows.standfirst: Over the past five years, a mortgage caste system developed in America. Realtor.com’s Hannah Jones sees cracks developing.

rows.title: JPMorgan’s nationwide home price forecast hides a Sunbelt full of pain. Watch out, Florida and Texas
rows.standfirst: JPMorgan Global Research sees prices falling quickest on the West Coast and in the Sunbelt.

rows.title: Cisco CEO Chuck Robbins says interviews for promotions are ‘stupid’— he cares more about whether your coworkers think you deserve a raise
rows.standfirst: Forget interview prep—the boss of the $340 billion tech giant Cisco believes employees on track for a promotion must get the approval of their peers.

rows.title: Seahawks head coach turned down a cushy career in finance at KPMG for a football internship—12 years later, he won the Super Bowl at 38
rows.standfirst: The Seattle Seahawks just won the Super Bowl—but their coach Mike Macdonald wouldn’t be bringing home a trophy if it weren’t for his gutsy career choice to ditch finance.

rows.title: AI could trigger a global jobs market collapse by 2027 if left unchecked, former Google ethicist warns
rows.standfirst: Former Google insider and AI expert Tristan Harris says without proper guardrails, AI could severely impact safety, security, and economic well-being.

rows.title: Americans are shocked by utility bills as high as $1,000: They’re paying the price for aging grids, fuel-price whiplash, and extreme weather
rows.standfirst: Many Americans are sharing monthly bills of over $1,000, cutting into their grocery budgets.

rows.title: It turns out that Joe Biden really did crush Americans’ dreams for the future. Just look at how the vibe changed 5 years ago
rows.standfirst: More than four in 10 Americans don’t anticipate “high-quality life” in five years’ time, the lowest mark in nearly 20 years

rows.title: Argentina’s 5 straight months of surging inflation undercount the severity, economists say
rows.standfirst: The formula that INDEC used to calculate inflation still underestimates real price rises in a country reeling from Milei’s harsh austerity program.

rows.title: Ex–Google exec says degrees in law and medicine are a waste of time because they take so long to complete that AI will catch up by graduation
rows.standfirst: “Higher education as we know it is on the verge of becoming obsolete,” the former Google AI leader told Fortune.

rows.title: Nightmarish labor market finally shows signs of letting up—and some ‘vindication’ for Jerome Powell
rows.standfirst: “Low-hire, low-fire” is so 2025-coded as January suggests companies may actually be hiring in 2026. This jobs report made Maria Bartiromo say, “Wow.”

rows.title: Meet the serial CEO taking over Kroger: He started his career stacking supermarket shelves and went all in on retail at 17 thanks to his persistent mom
rows.standfirst: Greg Foran is now in charge of Kroger; he started working in retail at 17 after his mom sent a Woolworths job ad his way.

rows.title: Wall Street’s top analyst sees something weird going on with gold and interest rates, and warns inflation risks are rewriting market logic
rows.standfirst: “Investors are anxious about the level of returns they get in traditional assets,” Apollo chief economist Torsten Slok told Fortune.

rows.title: The Gen Z job nightmare is so bad that even billionaires are worried their kids won’t be able to keep a job, says wealth advisor to the 0.1%
rows.standfirst: It’s a “very real concern” for the ultrawealthy that their children aren’t prepared for the future, wealth adviser Tom Thiegs told Fortune.

rows.title: Turns out the U.S. economy didn’t create half a million jobs last year. It was just 181,000
rows.standfirst: It was the weakest year for jobs creation since the pandemic year of 2020, according to the January jobs report.

rows.title: Trump’s immigration curbs will help take 2.4 million people out of the workforce, but he’s betting AI can pick up the slack
rows.standfirst: Can AI make up lost productivity from crashing fertility rates and shrinking immigration flows? Trump will certainly hope so.

rows.title: The affordability crisis is driving unprecedented price cuts in the housing market, Realtor.com says
rows.standfirst: “Builders are clearly responding to today’s affordability pressures,” said Realtor.com chief economist Danielle Hale.

rows.title: Marriott’s CEO identifies a ‘fundamentally permanent shift’ for Americans: Even low-income families are stubbornly hanging on to vacations
rows.standfirst: Anthony Capuano says Americans are stubbornly hanging on to vacations.

rows.title: American home buyers are still on strike as lower mortgage rates are no match for sinking January sales
rows.standfirst: Home buyers aren’t warmer up to a mortgage rates.

rows.title: Layoffs and unemployment are quite low, actually, says BLS
rows.standfirst: Applications for jobless aid for the week fell by 5,000 to 227,000 from the previous week, the Labor Department reported Thursday.

rows.title: Middle-class Americans are paying for the data center and AI boom with higher electric bills and even food costs, Goldman Sachs warns
rows.standfirst: The data center push is a one-two punch for everyday Americans with the potential to slash consumer spending and even drive down U.S. GDP growth, according to the bank.

rows.title: Actress Jennifer Garner just took her $724 million organic food empire public. She started her career making just $150 weekly as a ‘broke’ understudy
rows.standfirst: Jennifer Garner went from being a “broke” theater understudy to starring in major Hollywood pictures. She took home $1 million last year in her role as cofounder.

rows.title: IBM is tripling the number of Gen Z entry-level jobs after finding the limits of AI adoption
rows.standfirst: Gen Z jobs aren’t dead yet: $240 billion tech giant IBM says it’s rewriting entry-level jobs—and tripling down on its hiring of young talent.

rows.title: Top analyst warns the economy is figuring out how to grow without creating new jobs, leaving a major vulnerability
rows.standfirst: The economy will grow because of higher productivity, aided in part by AI, says Michael Pearce of Oxford Economics. But people aren’t core to that story.

rows.title: AI is everywhere except in the data, suggesting it will enhance labor in some sectors rather than replace workers in all sectors, top economist says
rows.standfirst: “Maybe there is a J‑curve effect for AI, where it takes time for AI to show up in the macro data. Maybe not.”

rows.title: Fox News’ Dana Perino’s advice for Gen Z graduates: Stop waiting for the perfect job and just start working
rows.standfirst: The former press secretary and “The Five” co-host urges Gen Z graduates to stop holding out for perfect roles and start building connections now.

rows.title: Meet the grandmother living out of a 400-ft ‘granny pod’ to save money and help with child care—it’s become an American ‘economic necessity’
rows.standfirst: 65-year-old Denise Martin is part of a growing movement of Americans buying affordable tiny homes to live close to family and cut costs—and the trend helps out working parents.

rows.title: Keke Palmer became a millionaire at 12—but even with $1 million, she’d still only pay $1,500 in rent and drive a Lexus: ‘I live under my means’
rows.standfirst: Other successful elites like Warren Buffett, Mitzi Perdue, and Mark Cuban live under their means in quaint houses and apartment rentals.

rows.title: One of Stanford’s original AI gurus says productivity liftoff has begun after doubling in 2025 amid transition to ‘harvest phase’ along J-curve
rows.standfirst: “We are transitioning from an era of AI experimentation to one of structural utility.”

rows.title: Mel Robbins says feeling stuck ‘doesn’t mean you’re broken’—it’s the biggest mindset mistake people over 40 make
rows.standfirst: Bestselling author Mel Robbins says exceptional people are those who pay attention to “all the details that most people ignore,” advising Gen Xers to get on board with tech.

rows.title: Brian Moynihan isn’t so worried about an AI jobs bloodbath, pointing to a 1960s theory that computers would end all management roles
rows.standfirst: “People wrote … in 1969 that there would be no managers left in business because the computer itself would eliminate the need for managers, because they just moved information. Well, guess what? We have 20,000 managers today at Bank of America,” Moynihan said.

rows.title: Jerome Powell is facing a ‘puzzlement’ of economic data, with contradictions likely to freeze any immediate action on the base rate
rows.standfirst: “Such confusion often leads to inertia, and we suspect that there will be no knee-jerk policy reaction to any of the week’s reports,” Oxford Economics’ Bob Schwartz wrote.

rows.title: Airbnb CEO says AI is ‘the best thing that ever happened to’ his company—he warns other founders: ‘If you don’t disrupt yourself, someone else will’
rows.standfirst: “If you don’t disrupt yourself, someone else will,” Airbnb CEO Brian Chesky warns founders, as AI becomes instrumental to the rental giant.

rows.title: Klarna’s CEO agrees with Dario Amodei. He thinks his white-collar workforce will shrink by a third by 2030
rows.standfirst: CEO Sebastian Siemiatkowski says attrition, not layoffs, is the reason behind the company’s smaller workforce.

rows.title: Why your boss loves AI and you hate it: Corporate profits are capturing your extra productivity, and your salary isn’t
rows.standfirst: As happened with the first factories of the Industrial Revolution, today’s AI boom is boosting output, but most of the gains are flowing to capital, not workers.

rows.title: Zillow’s CTO says AI is reinventing every step of the home buying process
rows.standfirst: Zillow’s CTO David Beitel has led technology for the real estate website since its inception, with his north star focused on infusing technology across all stages of the home buying process.

rows.title: Shocked Zillow CEO says even senior hires don’t do their homework for interviews: ‘They’re asking pretty basic questions that you could answer in 10 minutes on Google’
rows.standfirst: Zillow CEO Jeremy Wacksman says it “still surprises” him when executive-level candidates haven’t done their homework.

rows.title: The billion-dollar justification: why AI giants need you to fear for your job
rows.standfirst: Ask yourself about the giant job-loss narrative: whose interests does this story suit?

rows.title: America faces a ‘debt crisis’ a lot like the 1980s when a ‘private pact’ brokered by Ronald Reagan did the trick
rows.standfirst: A bipartisan commission saved Social Security in the 1980s. How would that approach fare today?

rows.title: The mortgage rate just hit its lowest level in over 3 years—and it’s still over 6%
rows.standfirst: Sept. 8, 2022, was the last time the average rate was below 6%.

rows.title: Entry-level tech and finance workers in Ireland are losing their jobs thanks to AI. Could that be a warning sign for the U.S.?
rows.standfirst: Youth job growth stays stagnant and unemployment is rising in Ireland in sectors AI is threatening to take over.

rows.title: Trump’s housing secretary moves to end ‘days of illegal aliens, ineligibles, and fraudsters gaming the system’
rows.standfirst: Advocates say tens of thousands face eviction if and when a new policy requiring them to show proof of citizenship is enforced.

rows.title: This math graduate applied to over 1,000 jobs and still didn’t hear back—so he moved to Austria
rows.standfirst: Gen Z and millennial workers in Britain are so fed up with being ghosted by employers that some are giving up on the country altogether.

rows.title: Something big is happening in AI, but that’s the only thing Matt Shumer got right
rows.standfirst: This could be the greatest democratizing event of all time.

rows.title: The ‘alternative scenario’ of an even bigger national debt disaster is in play after the Supreme Court ruled Trump’s tariffs illegal
rows.standfirst: Federal debt was set to reach 120% of GDP by 2036, the CBO projected, but that assumed the tariffs would stay in place.

rows.title: Former Goldman Sachs CEO Lloyd Blankfein says Peter Thiel is wrong: College is worth it because it makes you a ‘complete person’
rows.standfirst: Former Goldman Sachs boss Lloyd Blankfein hit back at tech leaders who say the degree is dead: Attending college is actually one of the best ways to open doors and grow confidence.

rows.title: Mark Cuban says AI won’t take your job anytime soon because it still acts like a hungover college intern—with a $100K price tag to show for it
rows.standfirst: As tech CEOs predict mass job displacement, billionaire former Shark Tank star Mark Cuban just revealed the “smartest counter” to that narrative.

rows.title: ‘We are in a dismal fiscal situation, and it just got worse’: Budget watchdog sounds the alarm even louder after Supreme Court erases Trump’s tariffs
rows.standfirst: Many shoppers and companies might cheer the drawdown of Trump’s tariffs, but the truth is America really needed that money.

rows.title: New CBO report shows national debt spiraling into uncharted territory by 2035—and Trump’s tariff defeat will make the picture even worse
rows.standfirst: By 2035, the CBO expects the deficit to reach $2.96 trillion or 6.2% of GDP versus 5.8% today, and almost double the multi-decade, pre-pandemic average.

rows.title: New Fed report proves Milton Friedman and Joe Biden understood something vital about immigration—and explains why growth may sputter under Trump
rows.standfirst: A new research paper found that the huge influx of foreigners under President Biden’s open border policy had the beneficial role of increasing the labor force, especially in areas where the U.S. sorely needed workers.

rows.title: Recruiter reveals broken Zoom interview etiquette: bathrobes, yoga, and outsourcing thinking to AI
rows.standfirst: Redballoon’s Sara Nibler said she recently screened a candidate who was “fresh from the shower, with his hair still dripping wet, his shirt was open.”

rows.title: Meet the retired Olympic champions starting second careers at Goldman Sachs with zero financial expertise and no office experience
rows.standfirst: Olympic champions and pro athletes are finding a new start at Goldman Sachs after retiring from sports. Luckily for them, the bank is looking for their distinct skills over their financial savvy.

rows.title: Last year, Accenture trained 550,000 workers in AI—now it’s warning senior staff to use it or don’t get promoted
rows.standfirst: Bosses have long warned staff to come to grips with AI. Now, companies like Accenture, KPMG, and Ring are tying employees’ AI usage to their future success and remuneration.

rows.title: Goldman Sachs says U.S. consumers are stuck with higher prices even after Supreme Court ruling opens door to $180 billion in tariff refunds
rows.standfirst: Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent expressed doubt that households would receive any money raised from tariffs: “I got a feeling the American people won’t see it.”

rows.title: Uber CEO predicts most rides could be robot operated within 20 years
rows.standfirst: Uber CEO Dara Khosrowshahi said business leaders must begin to contend with the encroaching AI job displacement wave.

rows.title: ‘Maya MacGuineas should be ashamed’: Scott Bessent launches war of words with the nonpartisan think tank that agrees with Trump on tariffs
rows.standfirst: For her part, MacGuineas said Bessent’s diatribe was “a bit of an odd response.”

rows.title: Below zero: Fed governor wouldn’t be surprised at negative job growth number
rows.standfirst: Christopher Waller warned that January’s 130,000 job pickup could have been a one-time deal.

rows.title: ‘It’s going to be painful for a lot of people’: Software engineers could go extinct this year, says Claude Code creator
rows.standfirst: Boris Cherny says Claude Code has been writing all of his code since November.

rows.title: Nearly half of companies are turning to poor ‘peanut butter’ raises—following the same pattern of the 2008 recession, an expert says. And it could take years to recover
rows.standfirst: Even if you land a job in the current market, peanut butter raises mean you probably won’t get a sizable raise. One expert warns that pay budget increases were stuck at about 3% for a long time after the Great Recession.

rows.title: Top economist says stock market has gotten ‘increasingly disconnected from the economy’
rows.standfirst: So much speculation in financial markets does not bode well for an “already vulnerable economy,” Mark Zandi warns.

rows.title: Home Depot CEO says with the housing market stalemate, ‘our customers are telling us that they’re not investing’
rows.standfirst: Ted Decker said on Tuesday’s earnings call that housing affordability issues were continuing to drive consumers away from home improvements.

rows.title: Ex–presidential candidate Andrew Yang warns that millions of white-collar workers will lose their jobs within 18 months: ‘The AI jobpocalypse is here’
rows.standfirst: AI is about to gut millions of office jobs, says ex–presidential candidate Andrew Yang. Even dog walkers, hairstylists, and restaurants will be impacted.

rows.title: America’s $901 billion trade deficit is like ‘chronically high cholesterol,’ top economist says, and Trump’s 150-day tariffs are the wrong medicine
rows.standfirst: Trump’s trade policy risks confusing one problem with a much bigger crisis, according to Harvard professor Gita Gopinath.

rows.title: Rolex has just opened a trade school for watchmakers in Texas. Already competition is as fierce as Harvard’s, and students could walk out with $95,000 jobs
rows.standfirst: Rolex is training college dropouts and disillusioned office workers to become watchmakers. More than 560 people applied for just 27 spots in 2024—a 4.82% acceptance rate, close to Harvard’s.

rows.title: Despite the constant ‘job apocalypse’ warnings, computer science graduates are actually on track to earn $81,000 right out of college
rows.standfirst: New data suggests that fears about the demise of computer science majors may be overblown—with demand outpacing MBAs and starting salaries growing year over year.

rows.title: Trump claims America is ‘winning so much.’ The IMF agrees, adding that Trump’s trade policies are the only thing holding it back from even more
rows.standfirst: The best time to chip away at the national debt and balance the budget is now, when the economy is strong, says the IMF. Trump’s trade tariffs are making that difficult.

rows.title: For the first time since 2022, the average U.S. mortgage rates is below 6%
rows.standfirst: As the annual spring home-buying season begins, it could encourage prospective home shoppers to get out there.

rows.title: How Zohran Mamdani and his fake newspaper charmed Trump, led to promise of major housing deal
rows.standfirst: The meeting on Thursday was previously unannounced and lasted for about an hour.

rows.title: Workers are making over $1 million by secretly holding down multiple gigs—and they’re doing it all within the 40-hour workweek
rows.standfirst: Holding multiple full-time jobs may sound impossible, but these overemployed remote workers are managing to squeeze in two to three jobs within a regular workweek—no overtime needed.

rows.title: More people are moving out of the U.S. than moving in for the first time since the Great Depression—a bad omen for the $38.8 trillion national debt
rows.standfirst: How Trump’s immigration crackdown could erase “the most potent fiscal engine this country has ever seen.”

rows.title: The week the AI scare turned real and America realized maybe it isn’t ready for what’s coming
rows.standfirst: From the “Ghost GDP” to mass layoffs at tech companies, this was the week AI’s new collar economy took full effect.

rows.title: Meet the Gen Z college students who turned Excel into a competitive esport—they’re competing in spreadsheet challenges and it’s helping them land jobs
rows.standfirst: Microsoft-backed spreadsheet competitions are turning Gen Z college students into job-market standouts.
